title: How the Bicycle Evolved
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: There are now more than a billion bicycles in the world, and few machines have changed so little in more than a century. Yet the bicycle took a long time to arrive. Its earliest ancestor appeared in 1817, when a German baron named Karl von Drais built a wooden machine with two wheels, a seat and a steering bar. It had no pedals. The rider simply pushed against the ground with his feet, rather like a child on a scooter, and the machine was nicknamed the hobby horse.

In the 1860s, inventors in France added pedals directly to the front wheel. This machine, called the velocipede, was much faster, but it was far from comfortable. Its wheels were made of wood and had iron rims, and on the rough roads of the time the rider was shaken so badly that people called it the boneshaker. It was popular for a few years with young, wealthy men, but most people considered it an expensive toy.

The next step was to increase the size of the front wheel. Because one turn of the pedals moved the machine a distance equal to the circumference of the front wheel, a bigger wheel meant a higher speed. By the 1870s, riders were perched on seats more than a metre above the ground on machines with front wheels over a metre and a half across. These high-wheelers, later nicknamed penny-farthings, were fast but dangerous. If the front wheel struck a stone, the rider was often thrown forward over the handlebars, and serious injuries were common.

The machine that we recognise today appeared in 1885, when an English maker named John Kemp Starley produced the Rover safety bicycle. It had two wheels of equal size, and the pedals drove the rear wheel through a chain, which meant that the rider could sit low and stay close to the ground. A few years later, in 1888, a Scottish vet named John Boyd Dunlop fitted his son's tricycle with tyres filled with air. They made the ride far smoother, and within a decade almost every bicycle used them.

The safety bicycle changed society as well as transport. It was cheap enough for workers to buy, so people could live farther from their jobs. It was especially important for women, who had little freedom to travel alone. The American campaigner Susan B. Anthony declared in the 1890s that the bicycle had done more for women's freedom than anything else in the world. Women began to wear shorter skirts and looser clothes so that they could ride, and clubs for cyclists sprang up in towns across Europe and America.

In the twentieth century the car pushed the bicycle to the edge of city life in many countries. It returned in the 1970s, when a sharp rise in oil prices made driving expensive, and its popularity has continued to grow. Cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam have built thousands of kilometres of separate cycle lanes, and electric bicycles, which have a small motor to help the rider on hills, have made cycling possible for people who once found it too tiring.

A modern bicycle is a simple machine. The rider sits on the saddle, steers with the handlebars and pushes the pedals. The pedals turn a chain, which drives the rear wheel. All the parts are held together by the frame, a diamond of light steel or aluminium tubes that is both strong and easy to repair. It is this simplicity, together with the fact that the rider supplies all the power, that makes the bicycle the most efficient means of transport ever invented.

items.s: The world now has more than a billion bicycles.
Von Drais's machine had pedals on the front wheel.
The velocipede was invented in Germany.
e: inventors in France added pedals directly to the front wheel

items.s: The velocipede was comfortable to ride on rough roads.
e: the rider was shaken so badly

items.s: The velocipede was popular with people of every income.
e: popular for a few years with young, wealthy men

items.s: A bigger front wheel gave a higher speed for each turn of the pedals.
e: a bigger wheel meant a higher speed

items.s: Penny-farthings were nicknamed after two coins.
items.w: The passage gives the nickname but does not explain it.

items.s: The Rover safety bicycle had wheels of the same size.
Dunlop first tested his tyres on a racing bicycle.
e: fitted his son's tricycle with tyres filled with air

items.s: Cycling clubs were formed in both Europe and America.
e: clubs for cyclists sprang up in towns across Europe and America

items.s: Electric bicycles are more expensive than ordinary bicycles.
e: electric bicycles, which have a small motor to help the rider on hills

e: added pedals directly to the front wheel

items.s: It was named for the way it shook its rider.
The rider sat more than a metre above the ground.
e: more than a metre above the ground

items.s: It used a chain to drive the rear wheel.
e: the pedals drove the rear wheel through a chain

items.s: Many riders were injured by falling over the handlebars.

items.q: Why was a larger front wheel used on high-wheelers?
o: It made the ride more comfortable.
It made the machine travel faster.
It made the machine easier to steer.
It allowed the use of a chain.
e: a bigger wheel meant a higher speed

items.q: What was the main advantage of the pneumatic tyre?
o: It lasted longer on rough roads.
e: They made the ride far smoother

items.q: Why did bicycle use increase again in the 1970s?
o: The price of oil rose sharply.
e: a sharp rise in oil prices made driving expensive
